**Darksiders **

Darksiders is a dark, brutal, and surprisingly atmospheric action-adventure game that blends intense combat with exploration, puzzles, and a strong apocalyptic setting.

You play as War, one of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, who returns to Earth only to find it completely devastated. Framed for starting the Apocalypse too early, War must uncover the truth while fighting his way through a world filled with demons, angels, and ancient forces.

The combat is fast and satisfying, with a great variety of weapons and abilities that make every encounter feel powerful. The game also does a great job of mixing combat with exploration and puzzle-solving, keeping the gameplay from becoming repetitive.

What makes Darksiders stand out is its atmosphere. The ruined cities, dark fantasy design, massive enemies, and comic-book-inspired visuals create a world that feels both violent and mysterious.

It may show its age in some areas, especially visually and mechanically, but its personality, world-building, and satisfying combat still hold up.

**Final verdict:** Darksiders is a stylish and underrated action-adventure that deserves attention from anyone who enjoys dark fantasy, brutal combat, and apocalyptic worlds.

[h1]TL;DR? See Conclusion[/h1]

[h1]INTRODUCTION:[/h1]
I got Darksiders because I was interested on the rather unique theme. Once I started playing it, I quickly found myself being oddly familiar, despite being my first playthrough. Then it dawned on me, the game played like other more popular Action Adventure titles such as, but not limited to: God of War, DMC, Zelda, Prince of Persia, Portal etc. At first I was skeptical about the similarities but still found Darksiders to be a fun game in it's own right.

[h1]PLOT (No Spoilers):[/h1]
War, one of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse has landed on Earth triggering a full scale conflict between Heaven and Hell which utterly disrupted the precious Balance that dominantly prevailed for eons. Hated by Hell, condemned by Heaven, War now walks the Earth in an attempt to clear his name.

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
+ Familiar but still Fun Gameplay: -Taking multiple inspirations from other titles, Darksiders takes the best of the best features and aspects of those titles and mashes them up to make a Frankenstein monster type of game which is unique unto itself. This game deserve more attention than what initially got.

+ Atmosphere and Sound: -Sound assets are magnificent, scenery are breathtaking and character art are wonderful built. They all come together to make a very immersive and beautiful post-apocalyptic Earth.

+ Graphics to Framerate Ratio: -Being a copy paste console port, does leave the game a bit weak in terms of graphical fidelity, poor texture quality, weak special effects and limited animations are blatantly visible but it does benefit older and more outdated PCs. The 1080p support does make it more vivid and sharp than the console counter parts.

+ Puzzles: Taking inspiration from the Zelda games, Darksiders does feature a lot of puzzle solving, involving different skill sets and items that the player acquire. The puzzles are simple enough to not be frustrating, yet delivers a certain level of complexity that makes them satisfying to solve.

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
- Controls: -Being a console port, this game was clearly designed to be played using a gamepad rather than the mouse and keyboard. Attempts were made to integrate it better to Keyboard controls but the player will be left rather frustrated for the most part.

- Limited Graphical settings: -This speaks for itself, the game hardly has any options to change graphical fidelity. If you find yourself using a lower-end PC and FPS drops occur, you probably won't be able to do anything about it.

- Poor Story and No character progression: -War is not the most likable video game personality you will encounter, the story does not develop on the main protagonist either in personality or traits. He will have the same expression and demeanor from start to finish. As the Fallout games say, "War never changes."

- Restrictive maps: -Lets make a checklist on what being a Horseman is all about. 1. Have a horse (albiet a bit late in the game but CHECK) 2. You can fight in said horse (CHECK) 3. You have a place to ride your Horse (NOT CHECK). The game gives you one or two maps where riding Ruin (your horse) viable, but other than those maps, you'll find yourself fighting on foot through small and cramped areas not being able to utilize the glory of mounted combat.

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]
GOOD GAME, it takes the best mechanics of other games and places them into one and making a very fun and enjoyable experience.

This franchise is a mix of different religions and ideas merged into a "what if" biblical end times scenario. You follow War, one of the four horsemen wrongfully blamed for the end times. Your motivation is simple. Prove your innocence and kill demons with simple hack and slash game play.

This game is what if “God of War” and “Zelda” had a baby. This game is also the best in the franchise. It is both short and to the point. Go to dungeon 1, solve the puzzles, kill the boss, repeat. This game is a short journey, but a worthwhile one if you like one of it's inspirations of “Zelda” or “God of War.”

Darksiders was one of the last generation’s hidden gems, a dark, beautifully designed pastiche of several other action-adventure titles. Planned as a four-part series, the franchise only got as far as Darksiders2 before publisher THQ declared bankruptcy in 2011, and its intellectual properties were sold off piece by piece. Most people who’ve played Darksiders were probably disappointed that THQ fell apart before the planned quadrilogy could be completed, as the two games we got were both highly entertaining, enjoyable action titles.

Each of the Darksiders games tells the story of one of the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse, and the first centers on War. War and his brothers act as enforcers for the Charred Council that maintains the balance between Heaven and Hell, keeping them in check until the third faction, humanity, is strong enough to provide a challenge to both sides. As the game opens, War finds himself called to Earth as Angels and Demons fight their way through the streets of a nameless city, but the squishy humans who reside there are no match for either. Clearly, he’s been summoned too early.

War fights his way through the streets until he comes up against a demon he can’t defeat, as it seems something is sapping his powers. He’s knocked unconscious and wakes up before a tribunal, accused of being the one responsible for kicking off Armageddon too soon and dooming humanity.

The story takes itself completely seriously, but there’s a disconnect between the heavy-handed narrative and the exaggerated visuals, and it can be hard to tell if Darksiders is being sincere or has its tongue planted in its cheek. The use of Christian end-times mythology as a backdrop for the story works well, and the chunky, colorful Joe Madureira designs resemble decked-out characters in World of Warcraft. Everything is edgy and over-the-top; there’s not a treasure chest in the game that doesn’t have at least three skulls in its design, and War’s enormous sword is known as the “Chaoseater.” Although this can feel overblown, it’s still fun. It gives Darksiders its own charm.

Darksiders borrows heavily from some of the best titles in the action and adventure genres, and although it’s imitative, it comes together to be more than the sum of its parts. Much of the gameplay is borrowed from The Legend of Zelda series, with dungeons that must be explored to find tools that aid in exploration and can also be used in combat. Beating a boss upgrades your life bar, and you literally collect the creatures’ hearts after besting one. The overworld’s visuals resemble Gears of War in their greyish-brown defiled beauty, and bosses might remind you of God of War or possibly Shadow of the Colossus. There’s even a dungeon later in the game that borrows ideas from Portal, with an item that shoots orange and blue rifts at special targets. You’ll come across some genre clichés, but for the most part, they’re fun ones. (A large, slow-moving elevator? Sure hope a bunch of mooks don’t jump in and start whaling on me.)

As I mentioned, neither the audio or the gameplay have been altered for this re-release. Thankfully, neither of these needed any changes. Liam O’Brien gives War a stoic, world-weary voice that sounds like he’s constantly holding back his rage, and Mark Hamill lends the Watcher the same voice as his Fear Feaster character from Adventure Time, basically Joker without the mirth. The boss’s voice lines are too few and spoken too frequently, but it’s a minor annoyance you probably won’t notice if you don’t get stuck on a boss fight.
 
I did run into some minor problems. During the first couple of hours, lip syncing didn’t quite match up during cutscenes, though this did self-correct after a while. Even though I was playing with a controller, the mouse pointer showed up center screen whenever I was shopping, no matter how many times I moved it offscreen.

Darksiders still holds up exceptionally well, and it’s easy to recommend. It’s not quite as fresh and exciting as it was in 2010, but I still think it’s something everyone should try out. If you’ve played it before, it’s worth revisiting. If you haven’t, it’s a solid adventure that’s well worth your time.

Verdict: 8/10

[h1]"In times of war, the law falls silent."
[i]~Marcus Tullius Cicero[/i][/h1]

The seventh generation of video game consoles. In my humble opinion, it was the last generation, in which console war was still a thing. I mean, seriously. Look at the world we live in now. We have [b]Kingdom Hearts[/b] and [b]Final Fantasy[/b] on [b]Xbox[/b], [b]Crash Bandicoot[/b] and [b]Forza[/b] on [b]PC[/b] and so on. Sure, technically, the console war is still on and some titles are still available only on certain platforms, but all in all, seventh generation was the last one when it was still interesting. The last one when it was actually worth having more than one system on you. And this game? It's taking advantage of that.

See, even up to this day we never had [b]The Legend of Zelda[/b] game outside [b]Nintendo[/b]'s system. We also never had [b]God of War[/b] game outside [b]PlayStation[/b] family. [b]Vigil Games[/b] decided to change that. Not by porting those games, of course (we all know what [b]Nintendo[/b] does with those who mess with their property, the guys are worse than any inquisition), but by making their own high quality alternative. That's pretty much all you need to know about the [b]Darksiders[/b]. It's stylish and charming mix between [b]The Legend of Zelda[/b] and [b]God of War[/b].

[b]Vigil Games[/b] didn't stop there, though. They literally took everything that was cool about popular titles like [b]Devil May Cry[/b], [b]Gungrave[/b], [b]Ubisoft[/b]'s [b]Prince of Persia[/b], [b]Legacy of Kain[/b], [b]Portal[/b] and even [b]WarCraft[/b] (design in this game was copied from what we had in [b]WarCraft III[/b] / [b]World of WarCraft[/b] almost as is), mixed all that together and called it a day. Sure, it doesn't sound that good. I mean... we all hate plagiarism, right? But you know what? It actually [i]is[/i] a good thing. Thanks to [b]Darksiders[/b], a lot of people who never played such games before finally got a chance to do so, while the others? The others just got even more of a good thing.

Like I said, [b]Darksiders[/b] is a high quality product. It looks good and it feels good. Almost as good as the original titles. And all of those different elements from different games? They work surprisingly well together. While playing as a brutal guy who looks almost exactly like [b]Arthas Menethil[/b], we'll explore a [b]Zelda[/b]-like world with dungeons, use a gun like [b]Dante[/b] and [b]Beyond the Grave[/b], do some basic tricks like in those early [b]Prince of Persia[/b] titles from [b]Ubisoft[/b], we'll fight some huge enemies and do [b]QTE[/b] like in [b]God of War[/b], solve the puzzles similar to what we had in [b]Zelda[/b], [b]Legacy of Kain[/b] and [b]Portal[/b], and so on. It really does work perfectly well. The addiction, the satisfaction... it's all here.

Add the fact that this game also comes with surprisingly great cast (not only we've got [b]Troy Baker[/b], we've also got [b]Mark Hamill[/b] himself, so, it's, like, one heck of a [b]Joker[/b] paradise here) and you'll see that... well... this game is good. Simple like that. You want a good game? Here it is. It's really hard to find something really bad to say about the [b]Darksiders[/b]. No matter how you look at it, it's a good game and that's it. Even the fact that [b]Vigil Games[/b] kind of overdid it with puzzles at one point can't change that (even though they sure did and this game comes with even more annoying dungeon than that [b]Water Temple[/b] thingy from [b]Ocarina of Time[/b], keep that in mind if you don't have enough patience).

There's one thing, though, that gives [b]Darksiders[/b] a certain... unpleasant aftertaste. I'm talking, of course, about the fact that this game doesn't have a face. Like [b]John Travolta[/b] in that certain [b]John Woo[/b] movie. Sure, it looks very impressive and stylish, but at the same time, when you look at this game? You don't see [b]Darksiders[/b]. You see the original games. When you watch cutscenes? It's a bloody [b]WarCraft[/b]. When you shoot? You see [b]Dante[/b]. When you pick up bombs from the ground? You see [b]Link[/b] who's getting ready to face [b]King Dodongo[/b]. And so on. The biggest problem with this game is that it can't really offer you anything unique, while everything that [b]Vigil Games[/b] borrowed from the other titles is so obvious that it's literally impossible not to think about that. It's just a bunch of some really cool stuff from the other, more famous titles and that's it. Does it ruin the game? Of course, not. And yet, like I said, it adds a certain unpleasant aftertaste. Like... you know. When you're playing one of those so-called “clones”, no matter how good it is, it's still just a clone, right?

There was a good chance to fix all that through story, bu-u-ut... let's just say that story is not the strongest point here. All in all, it's fine, but it relies too much on setting. You know, angels, demons, post-apocalyptic future... In other words, it's [b]Requiem: Avenging Angel[/b]. Which is pretty cool and stylish, but... let's just say that the actual storytelling is not really that good. [b]Vigil Games[/b] tried to follow the [b]God of War[/b] formula, in which our character just keeps beating the heck out of one character after another, but... let's just say that without [b]Kratos[/b] and his charisma you can't help but want more twists. I'm not trying to say that [b]War[/b] (yes, we're playing as one of the Horsemen of the Apocalypse here, because... you know... [b]War[/b]... [b]God of War[/b]... good grief...) isn't a charming character. It's just... it doesn't make as much impact as [b]Kratos[/b]. At least, not enough to cover for the lack of plot twists. In other words, the story just can't cover the fact that this game is just a clone. Unfortunately.

Then again, for those of us who don't have any consoles on them, this game is a great choice. And even for those who already played all of the games I've mentioned above, I can still recommend this one. Because, let's just admit it, having a good clone from time to time? It's a good thing. Like, OK, [b]Age of Empires[/b] is a good game. But it doesn't mean that we can't enjoy clones like [b]Star Wars: Galactic Battlegrounds[/b], [b]War Diary II[/b] and even [b]BC Kings[/b] because why the heck not? And [b]Darksiders[/b]? It's sure a good clone. Seriously, guys, you haven't played it yet? Go buy it.

[b]P.S.[/b] Nowadays, though, it may actually be a good idea to go for so-called [b]Warmastered Edition[/b] instead. The new version comes with the [b]4K[/b] resolution support (in the original version you can't go higher than [b]2K[/b]), high resolution textures, improved shadows and post-processing effects, re-rendered cutscenes and, the best of all, the pre-order weapon (the [b]Harvester[/b] scythe) as a free bonus. Well, it won't be [i]free[/i], since you'll need to buy it with the in-game currency, but you know what I mean. In [b]Warmastered Edition[/b] you won't need any pre-order codes to get [b]Harvester[/b]. In other words, it's, like, the same exact thing, only better and with pre-order bonus as a gift. Which makes purchasing the original version kinda useless. As long as you're not a die-hard geek who wants to have every single version of this game. Dixi.

I have completed Darksiders three times now. It doesn't really amaze me as a game in any way. The graphics are cartoonish and just about worthy of the Xbox 360 (not a compliment), the gameplay is formulaic and platformy reminiscent of a PlayStation 2 game (that's sort of a compliment) and the story-line and script is about as impressive as Michael Bay at his best (not really a compliment either), although having said that its "twist" ending keeps things at least a little fresh.

Despite all this, to this day I find something in Darksiders simplicity that I like. Maybe it is simply the pleasure in experiencing the humble origins of its overly-ambitious sequel, perhaps it's the idiosyncratic lore-rich post-apocalyptic Earth, or maybe it's the storyline - the idea of ageless god-like creatures on a self-serving mission to resurrect the annihilated human race. 

There is nothing new or groundbreaking about Darksiders, and although it was one of THQ's larger releases it is not at all a game that was made to be a money spinner I don't think. Somebody loved Darksiders, and in 2016 I still do. The level design is varied in a predictable sort of way (forest level, desert level, city level, scary level), the bosses which you hunt are quite interesting but again nothing new (giant spider, giant bat) and a lot of the game's completion relies on that obsession with collectables and point gathering that 2006-2010 games are so infamous for. 

This game is totally charming. And it did give us the bug-riddled but excellent Darksiders II. If you are a fan of the latter or you think that the Playstation 2 was the best games console to grace God's green Earth, pick up this game.

Darksiders 1 is one of those rare games that ages like fine wine. Even years later, it still stands strong thanks to its atmosphere, story, and gameplay balance.

You play as War, one of the Four Horsemen, in a ruined, apocalyptic world that feels heavy, lonely, and epic at the same time. The art style is bold and dark, inspired by comic books, and it gives the game a unique identity that still looks amazing today.

The combat is brutal and satisfying—mixing hack-and-slash action with meaningful upgrades and abilities. Every new weapon or power actually changes how you fight, not just your damage numbers. Boss fights feel massive and memorable, exactly how they should in a game about gods and demons.

What really makes Darksiders special is how it blends Zelda-style puzzles and exploration with action combat. Dungeons are well-designed, puzzles make you think without being annoying, and progression feels rewarding.

The soundtrack and voice acting (especially War’s voice) add so much weight and seriousness to the experience. The story is simple but powerful—about honor, betrayal, and balance—and it pulls you in until the end.

I forget how I came to be in possession of Darksiders, or even how I became aware of it. But I do know that I first played it on Xbox 360 and it is a shining example of what a "Triple-A" release can be if it is allowed to: A game that has almost nothing new but does almost everything right. It's a fusion of PS2-era God-of-War-style hack-and-slash combat with Zelda-style dungeon crawling and equipment gathering, dressed up in a comic-book retelling of the biblical apocalypse, with bulging muscles and growling voices, born from the mind of noted X-Men author Joe Madureira. Darksiders is a spectacle of visual effects and button mashing that looks ridiculous on the surface- but it absolutely works in practice. As a life-long non-fan of the Zelda series, my frequent refrain is that Darksiders is my favorite iteration. 

The player takes the role of no-one less then War, horseman of the apocalypse. Banished to a wasted Earth following a premature triggering of Armageddon, for which he has been blamed, War must tear his way through demons, angels, the walking dead and towering monstrosities to discover the truth. He has his trusty sword Chaoseater and horse Ruin, a variety of other weapons and magic artifacts, and help from small handful of non-hostile NPCs. 

A lengthy and meaty game without excessive difficulty, Darksiders is an entertaining romp and certainly one of the better large titles of it's generation. It would then be exceeded by it's sequel, this time starring Death and taking on an Action-RPG bent with upgradable weapons and armor, new worlds beyond Earth and a quest system.

The death of THQ cast the future of the series in doubt, though not forever, as there is now a much-awaited third entry in the series that I have yet to play. But I will.

Some people refer to Darksiders as "Zelda meets God of War." I don't think they mean it in a bad way at all because the game is far different enough from those two to make it's mark as a distinguished title.

The comparison to Zelda and God of War are in reference to the fact that this is an action-adventure game with combat similar to God of War and puzzles similar to Zelda. As I said earlier though, this game is different enough from those two that it makes for a fairly unique game experience. Few action games have the kind of puzzles present in this game and almost no puzzle based games feature the combat that Darksiders has. 

Even though it's different in it's own way than God of War, if you have played GoW you'll feel right at home with the controls and the combat. You have your basic attacks, magic, and a huge number of combos to pull off. Countering enemies is always satisfying and gives you a huge advantage in that moment. Bosses are also great with each providing a slightly different mechanic to use to defeat them.

One area where I feel the game could improve is the ratio of combat to puzzles. There were some puzzle sections that seemed to go on just a hair too long as I was itching to kill more stuff. Combat is so fun that you end up missing it when doing the puzzle sections (which are adequate, but not quite up there with Zelda). This slightly breaks up the flow of the game and as I said earlier some puzzle stages definitely overstay their welcome. It doesn't help that the puzzles are usually somewhat mediocre (move x to y, push button, etc.). They aren't bad, but it's not like the combat which in itself is pretty exceptional.

On a visual level this is a relatively old game but it still looks pretty good thanks to Todd McFarlane's excellent character designs. Character design is great and you truly get the sense of being in a fantasy/post-apocalyptic setting. Some visual effects are absent as this game was made awhile ago and unfortunately cut scenes are not in 1080p.

Puzzles and visuals aside this is one great game. It's fun and challenging without being frustrating and combat is a blast (when you're not solving puzzles). As far as achievements go there are a number of collectibles in the form of upgrades so they are worth collecting even if you need a guide. A forewarning about achievements in this game though: Some will NOT unlock when they should so keep your eye on the corner of your screen when you expect to get an achievement. I found I had to go back several times to pick up an achievement for beating a boss or collecting an item so make a LOT of saves if you can. This doesn't break the experience though and it only happened a few times so I would still give it a shot at getting 100% if you're up for that sort of thing. 

With great combat and a unique art style (even with dated graphics) Darksiders is a great experience. There really isn't too much else out there like it and it will keep you busy for awhile (15-20 hours).

This game is pretty badass. It plays like a mixture of Zelda and God of War/Devil May Cry/Bayone- Look, you do puzzles and crazy combo attacks, and sometimes you press a button/key to rip some poor soul's limbs off. It is, for the most part, mindless entertainment (other than the puzzles and the brief strategy involved in the combat).

The story is based on the Judeo-Christian Apocalypse and one member of its heralds, War of the Four Horsemen, accidentally starting the end of the world too soon. It quickly becomes a story of revenge, justice, and answers as War travels across a destroyed earth (or, more accurately and area that could easily be just what/where New York City and some part of New Jersey used to be. It's not the full planet) taking down other biblical beasts and monsters of both Heaven's and Hell's host. If I am not mistaken, War is actually described as, "Hunted by Heaven, and Hated by Hell."
While its fun, it is a bit straight forward up until the end, in which you're thrown a few twists and turns.

Speaking of being straight forward, the game is fairly linear, but in a more Zelda-y or Halo: CE sense than a Call of Duty and FINAL FANTASY XIII way. You're given many areas (Forgive me for not remembering the exact number, it's actually been months since I played the game) to explore in a pseudo-open world sense, with at least one dungeon per area. In the dungeons, you go back and forth between combat and solving puzzles to progress, and like in Zelda, acquiring a new skill or tool to complete the dungeon and open up old paths for exploration in the other areas.

I know I keep referencing Zelda, and while some might consider that to be a bad thing, I certainly don't. I love that franchise, and the only reason I keep alluding to it is because it's a forerunner in its field (kinda), and it really is the best comparison I can make with this game. I'm sure there are a bunch of other puzzle-y, platform-y, RPG-ish games out there that have the same feel as Darksiders, but I just don't know them.

Anyway, the sound design is pretty damn spot on. Things squish, crunch, rip and smash in brutally good sounding ways, and War sounds like the embodiment of destruction should. Oh, and Mark Hamil has a voice in this game, and he's always welcome because, well, hell, it's Luke GOSHDANG Skywalker and The Joker (and Skips). The demons sound demonic, the angels sound pious and righteous, and the music... Um. The music didn't stand out to me, at least not like the sequel's does. It was adequate. Enough for a post-apocalyptic action game.

The art design is definitely one of my favorite aspects of this game, and the sequel too. It's all comic book-y, and I love it. There's plenty of realism in the environment and some of the characters, but not enough that it looks like it's trying too hard, and not too little to the point that it feels like I'm defintely looking at a cartoon.

Now, there is leveling and a small degree of customization involved in the game, but I quickly found a weapon I wanted (which do not present themselves too often) and loaded it with the skill I liked the most (health absorption and DoT, mainly), so I didn't really delve too deeply into the game's RPG elements. Oops (look, this is my first big review, and like I said, it's been a while. Please don't kill me).

It's aesthetic choices are divisive to say the least.

Fortunately, the gameplay is solid. Again, that's mainly because Darksiders is a blatant LoZ clone. However, it at least has the decency to be a competent one. There's a lot of effort and care put into the puzzles and enemies that populate the game's varied dungeons. It offers nothing revolutionary, but Darksiders constantly strives to match the quality of its predecessors. And honestly, there aren't many games I can honestly cay make so sincere an effort.

The end of the world has already happened—you just weren't the one who started it. Or were you?

Darksiders drops you into the shattered boots of War, one of the Four Horsemen, as he fights to clear his name in a world where Heaven and Hell have already begun tearing each other apart. It's a story fueled by revenge, betrayal, and the search for the truth, wrapped in one of the coolest fantasy settings gaming has ever seen.

The combat is brutal without becoming repetitive, mixing heavy swordplay, satisfying combos, and supernatural abilities that make every encounter feel rewarding. But what truly surprised me wasn't the fighting—it was the dungeon design. Every area feels handcrafted, packed with puzzles, hidden paths, and tools that make exploration just as enjoyable as battle.

The art style deserves its own praise. Even years later, the oversized armor, ruined cities, towering demons, and gothic atmosphere still look incredible. It doesn't chase realism, and that's exactly why it has aged so well.

Sure, some mechanics feel a little dated, but they never overshadow what Darksiders does best: delivering an unforgettable action-adventure that knows when to let you think, when to let you explore, and when to let you unleash absolute chaos.

If you've somehow missed this classic, it's still worth answering the call of the Horseman.

With the brutality hallmarks of God of War, the dungeon layout, items and puzzle and world concepts of more recent Legend of Zeldas, and the dark and epic story that best recalls the weighty dialogue of the Legacy of Kain games, this game is something of an amalgamation.  And that's a good thing, because instead of simply taking those elements as they are (which is good enough as it is), this game takes all those elements and weaves them into an action adventure game where basically every moment is your character looking, sounding, and feeling like a badass.  In every detail, the position of the main character as a Horseman of the Apocalypse is never in question; your power is even evident in how the character walks and lands when jumping.  To be paired with this, the beautiful post apocalyptic world you explore is similarly fleshed out.  If you yearn for a solid, thorough action adventure game akin to the aforementioned games, this is more than worth a purchase.

One quick note, as an aside: there IS a quick way to amass souls once you finish the Ashlands.  YouTube would be the best place to look this up; it is heartily helpful for those that, like me, desire every powerup you can get in a game. ;)

[h1]Darksiders[/h1]

Darksiders is primarily a hack and slash action game developed by The Vigil Games and produced by THQ Nordic in the year 2010. It is based on the biblical story of  the arrival of four horsemen of Apocalypse to end the battle between Heaven's Hellguard and Hell's legions to maintain the balance whenever the seven seals are broken.

[h1]"The Seventh Seal Is Not Broken"[/h1]

The game starts off with Earth being a battleground for a barbaric war between angels and demons.Our protagonist WAR( the youngest among the horsemen) arrives to put an end to the Apocalypse.But to his surprise he doesn't find his brothers joining him in this cleansing act.

Confused and angry WAR wreaks hell on anything that comes in his path, killing a large number of heaven's and hell's forces without any hesitation. Soon he ends up fighting a giant mechanical monster called destroyer and during this fight he overhears the conversation between two angelic leaders of their plan to bring the apocalypse on Earth without breaking the seventh seal.

Furious and filled with rage WAR charges at the Destroyer but is easily overpowered and mocked. Seemingly killed during this brutal battle WAR finds himself saved by the Charred Council ( the entites charged by the creator to ensure balance). WAR pleads them of a wicked trickery and manages to get their allowance to uncover the truth and prove his innocence.Will WAR survive the hostile Apocalyptic Earth and its challenges to raise the curtains from a well devised plan or will he succumb, which is left to the player to find out and enjoy this roller coaster of a apocalyptic ride.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

Players control WAR through a third person perspective where the game requires players to fight hordes of varied enemies and engrossing boss battles. Another aspect of the game is puzzle soving which needs the usage of correct equipment at the right time to progress through the levels.

Throughout the game there are a number of scattered Vulgrim shops which can be accessed to improve or buy new gear in exchange of souls received by killing opponents. There are also parts in the game where WAR can summon his horse Ruin to assist him in combat and is absolutely essential while facing some specific boss battles.

Combat is the usual hacking and slashing, along with some ground shattering earthquake intensity punches. Different types of weapons for different playstyles are instilled to avoid repetitiveness. Along with combat comes blocking and dash which is needed to avoid incoming attacks or to send a devastating counter blow.

[h1]Graphics and Sounds[/h1]

Graphics and sound quality of this game fail to produce the desired effect. Even with the presence of different play areas the visuals are boringly same all around with exception to a few select areas such as Eden which is visitable only once throughout the game.  On the contrary the cutscenes of Darksiders are really well done and are quite motivating for a player to explore the game. The music and in game music gets irritating really soon and there is no major change in this field till the game ends.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
 [list]
  [*]Interesting plot.
  [*]Satisfactory and enjoyable combat.
  [*]Awesome Boss Battles.
  [*]Well created cutscences.
 [/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
 [list]
  [*]Repetitive gameplay and low replayability.
  [*]Music is well created.
  [*]Mediocre graphics.
  [*]Slow mechanics of WAR and under use of Ruin.
 [/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Darksiders is a good enough game to enjoy for the gamers having a taste of Hack-Slash with a really captivating story line. It does lack big time in some areas but it can surely be enjoyed for the first time around. I would recommend it to specific gamers with a liking of fast paced action. The game does have an awesome ending which generates interest for the second Darkisder game.

Man.. What do I say about Darksiders.. Well, it is by no means a bad game. The gameplay and combat are clean; the puzzles are intriguing enough; the voice acting is fairly well done (especially work done by Mark Hamill); and most enemy designs are intuitive and fun to fight. Speaking of enemies, instant killing enemies is such a joy!
 
However...

Darksiders is woefully uninspired. There is absolutely NOTHING original about this game. Everything about the combat, the puzzles, the level/game design, the level up schematic, and even the way you ride your horse (which you won't do very often) is borrowed from other game designs. If you have every played God of War and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time you will quickly pick up on the tropes and cliches that this game uses. Also, the bosses are simple and gimmicky. Not to mention that the game is fairly easy, even on hard. Lastly, the lore is mildy interesting but the plot and story execution are weak and it just feels like set up for the sequel. 

Final Word: 
Don't take my criticism as me not liking the game. I did enjoy it but it is far from being a great game. If you like linear hack and slash action games like God of War and Devil May Cry then you will enjoy this game. However, if you are looking for something fresh, new, and innovative, then Darksiders simply won't fit the bill. 

P.S I recommend playing with a controller; better layout and feel.

Darksiders is one of the first games, which combines two different types of games. That types are slasher and RPG, in some moments this combination is made well, but also there are some things that I find irritating. But about the story now, in this game we play as one of the horsemen of the apocalypse, he is called War. At the start of the game, we are killed by the demon, but after that, we come back to life after the year out of knowing what was happened in the world. We have been returned to life by Council, they said us what was happened, with that knowledge to get our honor back, we have to restore the balance of the world. To be sure that we will do it, Council gives the power above us to observe. In the whole of the game, developers give us some perfect plot twists, the last of them made truly smile on my face, it's because we get cut scene that shows what will happen at the end, after that, I felt so disappointed, but that plot twist made it the best end of the game, which could ever imagine. Also in-game was the moment that made me laugh, it's the moment in dialogue after we killed the second boss. Now some words about type game combination, that developers use to make Darksiders. About the good sides of that type of game combination, in the whole of the game we're able to fight with one main weapon, two secondary weapons, and six additional gear and equipment. The more we use a main or secondary weapon to fight, the much they are getting more powerful, every they can have a maximum fourth level of power. Even, if we upgrade all weapons to level four, we can make them stronger, to do it we're using special runes, all of them gives different passive, or active bonuses to fight. About the bad aspects of that idea, things we get from chests. In-game we have three types of souls, these are: blue, it's our currency, we can buy everything with using it, all additional moves upgrades, special attacks, and many types of crystals (remember that last thing), green gives us health, and orange gives us fury. So why things in chests are bad in my opinion? The answer is: In the game are many of chest, at some moments are four chests next to each other, and all of them almost always have only souls and that's why many times we take only two of them, rest of them most will not be open forever. In-game as I said before we have many types of crystals in it are health crystals, but we're able to find only about four of them in chests, okay but we can buy them, yes, but there is the main problem they are expensive. We get additional items but we can't use them, because it's completely unprofitable for us. At the end here are some tips about achievements. First, you can end the game with all achievement after one passing the game, to do it you have to choose the apocalyptic difficulty of the game, it will give you some problems at the beginning, but while you're further, the game start being easier (calmly you can die as much as you need to pass the game). Second, to get an achievement called Aerial Predator, to get it you have to kill one hundred and sixty, while you fly on the flying beast. It's not hard, but there is some problem with it. If you forget to make a save before the sequence has started, do it as fast as you can, if you didn't kill enough enemies, or you just die, you must load your save and go back to the main menu of the game, then choose to continue the game. The last one, the achievement is called Dark Rider. To get it you must ride one hundred miles on the horse, it's not hard but here is one problem, the counter can glitch so easy, so when you only get your horse don't get off him and just ride around the arena it's the safest way to do it, even the counter get a glitch, you can load save in which you're at the moment before you get the horse and try to do achievement again. The biggest criticism is that Darksiders doesn't do anything new, but combining all these great elements from other games so successfully IS something new.

Small semi disjointed plot summary:

The armies of heaven and hell wage an endless war. This war was stopped by the charred council and its enforcers, the four horsemen. Eventually a third race, that of man was discovered. Man became the peace timer, for once these weak yet cunning creatures were ready to take their place in the grand scheme of things, the seven seals would be broken, the war would resume and four horsemen would rain judgement down on all three sides.

Safe to say, shit hits the fan like a riding horsemen. You play as War, supposedly the strongest horsemen (measured purely in physical strength) and go down to earth do your job, only to notice your fellow horsemen haven't been summoned as well. And the shit keeps snowballing down hill.

Let's start off with the good:

The combat (the thing you shall be doing for most of this game) feels amazing, when you hit something, you feel like 
you've really hit something.

Combos feel nice.

There is decent variety in weapons and combos. (despite the fact I only used one of these weapons in real combat.)

Characters were overal pretty good. Though there are very few side characters, they do all serve a purpose.


Next up the mediocre:

The puzzles are meh, the real problem with them is that you are given no real hints, the best you get is a panning shot that hints vaguely in the general direction of the answer. 

The boss fights aren't all that interesting, doing the whole "do it three times and it dies" thing for the most part. Though there are the "bash it ti'll it's dead" bosses. It was hard to distinguish between those and a health bar for therm would have been nice. 

Enemy variety is a bit lacking. (I do not consider a colour change and some more health and damage as "variety.")

The story isn't all that amazing either, but it's servicable and works for the most part.

None of these things were a deal breaker for me.


The bad:

The game (at least for me) handled alt tabbing badly, to the point of crashing when I did, on occasion, alt tab. (my guess is that this was the reason some of my achievements didn't get counted.)


I do recommend this game though, it's not perfect, but nothing is and if you can live with the flaws it has, it's a good game.
